query.original_query: linguistic relativity color grammatical gender number LLM concept representation counterfactual language

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of linguistic relativity color perception grammatical gender and number concepts in large language models, counterfactual language probing feature analysis
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how large language models internally represent linguistic relativity effects, specifically probing for color perception biases and grammatical gender-number concepts through counterfactual language analysis. Using activation patching and causal tracing on multiple transformer-based models, we analyze the residual stream and MLP layers for features encoding grammatical gender agreement and number marking across languages with differing typological structures. Our analysis reveals that models exhibit localized feature representations for grammatical gender that interact with color term embeddings, consistent with weak linguistic relativity effects. We find that counterfactual probes—where grammatical gender or number is altered in input sentences—produce measurable shifts in downstream color similarity judgments, particularly in early-to-middle layers. Feature decomposition via sparse autoencoders identifies monosemantic features for feminine and masculine gender markers, as well as singular-plural distinctions, which partially absorb into broader semantic clusters. Results show that these internal representations are not fully separable from conceptual color spaces, suggesting that language-specific grammatical categories subtly modulate perceptual feature geometry in the model’s latent space.

sub_queries.semantic_query: linguistic relativity effects of color categorization grammatical gender and number marking on cognition, Sapir-Whorf hypothesis counterfactual language processing
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the influence of grammatical gender and number marking on non-linguistic cognitive processes, testing predictions derived from the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis. Participants whose native languages differ in the obligatory marking of grammatical gender (e.g., Spanish, German) and number (e.g., English, Japanese) completed a series of non-linguistic tasks, including similarity judgments for color categories and a visual search paradigm for object categorization. We measured reaction times and accuracy in a counterfactual reasoning task, using a novel adaptation of the false-belief paradigm to assess whether linguistic marking of hypothetical states modulates cognitive processing. Results indicate that speakers of languages with grammatical gender showed faster categorization of objects whose gender assignment matched the target’s grammatical class, consistent with a Whorfian effect on object classification. However, performance on the counterfactual reasoning task did not differ significantly across language groups. Findings support the hypothesis that habitual linguistic categorization can influence perceptual and conceptual processing in domain-specific ways, but do not provide evidence for a universal effect of language on counterfactual thought.

papers.title: Don’t Forget About Pronouns: Removing Gender Bias in Language Models Without Losing Factual Gender Information
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle and remove gender bias from language model representations while preserving factual gender information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using orthogonal probes to disentangle and filter gender bias from contextual language model representations while preserving factual gender information, showing bias can be reduced without significantly harming language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: It is possible to decrease stereotypical gender bias in language model representations while preserving factual gender information, without significant deterioration of the model's language modeling capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
The method decreases gender bias in profession names (measured by MSE) while preserving factual gender information for gendered nouns.
Filtering bias dimensions only moderately decreases masked language modeling accuracy on general text.
Preserving factual gender dimensions in the filter can improve pronoun prediction accuracy in coreference tasks by removing confounding stereotypical bias.
Probing identifies sparse dimensions in the embedding space that encode bias and factual gender information.
The method works on multiple transformer-based masked language models (BERT and ELECTRA).
papers.limitation:
The method does not remove all gender information, so downstream classifiers could still retrieve gender, making it unsuitable for tasks using gender-biased data.
The method does not fully remove gender bias; some bias remains in the representations.
The linear probe may not capture non-linear encoding of gender signals in the Transformer, and information might be recovered in subsequent layers.
papers.abstract: The representations in large language models contain multiple types of gender information. We focus on two types of such signals in English texts: factual gender information, which is a grammatical or semantic property, and gender bias, which is the correlation between a word and specific gender. We can disentangle the model's embeddings and identify components encoding both types of information with probing. We aim to diminish the stereotypical bias in the representations while preserving the factual gender signal. Our filtering method shows that it is possible to decrease the bias of gender-neutral profession names without significant deterioration of language modeling capabilities. The findings can be applied to language generation to mitigate reliance on stereotypes while preserving gender agreement in coreferences. 1

papers.title: Predicting and Explaining French Grammatical Gender
papers.research_question: How to predict and explain French grammatical gender using interpretable neural models with a global surrogate approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces interpretable neural models for French grammatical gender prediction, using a global surrogate approach with auxiliary attributes to provide tunable explanation complexity.
papers.conclusion: Orthography predicts the grammatical gender in French with high accuracy, and adding semantic features can improve this prediction. The black-box embedding can be explained by simpler decision tree models over a given auxiliary explanation space, both locally and globally.
papers.key_findings:
Orthography alone achieves 92.5% accuracy in predicting French grammatical gender.
Adding semantic information improves accuracy to 94.01%.
Phonological features provide less predictive power than orthography in French.
Feminine gender nouns are more explainable than masculine nouns due to more specific rules.
Global explanations lead to fewer overall rules but are more complex per instance, while local explanations are more accurate but may have inconsistent rules.
papers.limitation: Local explanations may lead to inconsistent rules for distant test points, which can be undesirable in applications like language learning.
future_direction: Cross-linguistic extension of the study
Human-in-the-loop curation for identifying new auxiliary attributes
papers.abstract: Grammatical gender may be determined by semantics, orthography, phonology, or could even be arbitrary. Identifying patterns in the factors that govern noun genders can be useful for language learners, and for understanding innate linguistic sources of gender bias. Traditional manual rule-based approaches may be substituted by more accurate and scalable but harder-to-interpret computational approaches for predicting gender from typological information. In this work, we propose interpretable gender classification models for French, which obtain the best of both worlds. We present high accuracy neural approaches which are augmented by a novel global surrogate based approach for explaining predictions. We introduce auxiliary attributes to provide tunable explanation complexity.

papers.title: Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is gender represented in multilingual models, and to what extent is the gender concept encoded in shared subspaces across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Gender representations in multilingual models consist of both shared and language-specific components, explaining why gender classification transfers well across languages but gender removal interventions do not.
papers.conclusion: Gender representation in multilingual models is partially shared across languages, with the most salient directions being shared, enabling transfer of classification, but language-specific directions prevent transfer of gender removal.
papers.key_findings:
Gender classification transfers very well across languages using linear probes.
Gender removal using Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) does not transfer well across languages.
Gender subspaces are spanned by a few dominant directions that are shared across languages and other language-specific directions.
The shared directions are the most dominant ones, enabling cross-lingual transfer of classification.
The partial sharing of gender directions explains the discrepancy between transfer of classification and removal.
papers.limitation: The study relies on a narrow notion of binary gender, which does not reflect the subtle ways by which gender bias is manifested.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models were shown to allow for nontrivial transfer across scripts and languages. In this work, we study the structure of the internal representations that enable this transfer. We focus on the representation of gender distinctions as a practical case study, and examine the extent to which the gender concept is encoded in shared subspaces across different languages. Our analysis shows that gender representations consist of several prominent components that are shared across languages, alongside language-specific components. The existence of language-independent and language-specific components provides an explanation for an intriguing empirical observation we make: while gender classification transfers well across languages, interventions for gender removal, trained on a single language, do not transfer easily to others.

papers.title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models encode gender bias in their internal representations, and how do debiasing techniques and fine-tuning affect this encoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals a consistent pattern of gender encoding in encoder-based language models (early layers suppress, later layers amplify) and shows that current debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, are often ineffective at reducing internal bias, while fine-tuning reduces gender information in representations but may concentrate bias in the classification head.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias is deeply embedded in pretrained language models, and current debiasing techniques are limited; proactive integration of fairness objectives during pretraining and targeted interventions in later layers are needed for effective mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Gender information follows a consistent encoding pattern across encoder models: early layers suppress gender signals, while later layers amplify them.
Debiasing techniques, particularly post-hoc methods, are often ineffective at reducing internal gender bias and can sometimes increase it.
Training-time Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) is the most effective debiasing method for reducing gender information compression.
Fine-tuning for a downstream task (occupation classification) reduces gender information in the encoder representations, but may shift bias to the classification head.
Larger models (e.g., BERT-large) tend to encode more gender information than smaller models (e.g., BERT-base).
papers.limitation:
Focus on gender bias in English-language biographies, leaving broader sociocultural and intersectional biases unexplored.
Study centers on encoder-based models; findings may not generalize to decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
The interplay between task-specific fine-tuning and bias propagation requires deeper exploration across diverse applications.
future_direction: Validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
Explore broader sociocultural and intersectional biases.
Investigate the interplay between fine-tuning and bias propagation across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Gender bias in pretrained language models (PLMs) poses significant social and ethical challenges. Despite growing awareness, there is a lack of comprehensive investigation into how different models internally represent and propagate such biases. This study adopts an information-theoretic approach to analyze how gender biases are encoded within various encoder-based architectures. We focus on three key aspects: identifying how models encode gender information and biases, examining the impact of bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning on the encoded biases and their effectiveness, and exploring how model design differences influence the encoding of biases. Through rigorous and systematic investigation, our findings reveal a consistent pattern of gender encoding across diverse models. Surprisingly, debiasing techniques often exhibit limited efficacy, sometimes inadvertently increasing the encoded bias in internal representations while reducing bias in model output distributions. This highlights a disconnect between mitigating bias in output distributions and addressing its internal representations. This work provides valuable guidance for advancing bias mitigation strategies and fostering the development of more equitable language models.

papers.title: The Birth of Bias: A case study on the evolution of gender bias in an English language model
papers.research_question: How does gender bias evolve during the training of a language model, and how do internal representations relate to downstream bias?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that gender bias in language models evolves through distinct phases during training, with gender information becoming increasingly localized in a single embedding unit, and that debiasing these embeddings can effectively reduce downstream bias, but with caution due to asymmetry in gender representation.
papers.conclusion: Monitoring training dynamics provides detailed understanding of bias evolution, and debiasing embeddings can be an effective mitigation strategy, but asymmetry in gender representation requires careful consideration to avoid introducing new biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gender representation in the model evolves through three phases: formation, consolidation, and specialization.
Gender information becomes increasingly localized in a single 'gender unit' in the input embeddings.
There is an asymmetry in how female and male genders are represented, with female tokens driving the development of the dominant gender unit.
Debiasing input embeddings using iterative null-space projection is effective in reducing downstream bias, especially later in training.
The correlation between input embedding bias and downstream bias changes over time, and dataset statistics like PMI correlate with bias.
papers.limitation:
Focus only on gender bias along a female-male axis, which is a simplification.
The study uses a relatively small LSTM model and may not generalize to larger models, Transformer architecture, other languages, or other biases.
future_direction: Generalize methods to larger language models, Transformer architecture, other languages, and other undesirable biases.
Overcome the simplification of gender as a binary.
papers.abstract: Detecting and mitigating harmful biases in modern language models are widely recognized as crucial, open problems. In this paper, we take a step back and investigate how language models come to be biased in the first place. We use a relatively small language model, using the LSTM architecture trained on an English Wikipedia corpus. With full access to the data and to the model parameters as they change during every step while training, we can map in detail how the representation of gender develops, what patterns in the dataset drive this, and how the model's internal state relates to the bias in a downstream task (semantic textual similarity). We find that the representation of gender is dynamic and identify different phases during training. Furthermore, we show that gender information is represented increasingly locally in the input embeddings of the model and that, as a consequence, debiasing these can be effective in reducing the downstream bias. Monitoring the training dynamics, allows us to detect an asymmetry in how the female and male gender are represented in the input embeddings. This is important, as it may cause naive mitigation strategies to introduce new undesirable biases. We discuss the relevance of the findings for mitigation strategies more generally and the prospects of generalizing our methods to larger language models, the Transformer architecture, other languages and other undesirable biases.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual models, and can counterfactual probing be used to causally manipulate this identity in embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in contextual token embeddings of multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to affect the language of generated tokens, but not specifically to boost translation-equivalent words, providing evidence for both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R contain both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing methods like AlterRep can be fruitfully applied to analyze and manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language systematically increases the probability of words from that language in masked language modeling.
Pushing embeddings away from the template language decreases the probability of words from that language.
The intervention does not specifically boost translation-equivalent words more than random words from the target language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language has minimal effect on target word probability but increases the overall prior for that language.
The method is robust to both monolingual and synthetic code-mixed training data.
papers.limitation:
INLP extracts only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed to manipulate non-linearly encoded properties.
The AlterRep procedure is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is tricky.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility, such as for machine translation.
The work carries the general risks associated with large language models, including environmental impacts.
future_direction: Use the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Apply more complex non-linear erasure methods, such as those proposed by Ravfogel et al. (2022).
Translate the findings into practical applications like machine translation.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs. We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R). We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y. Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task. We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language. But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models. Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component. And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the linear representation hypothesis be extended to represent categorical and hierarchical concepts in large language models, and how are hierarchical relationships encoded geometrically in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: Extends the linear representation hypothesis to represent binary features as vectors and categorical concepts as polytopes, and proves that hierarchical relationships between concepts are encoded as orthogonality in the representation space.
papers.conclusion: The representation space of large language models encodes hierarchical semantic structure through a simple direct sum of polytopes, where hierarchical relations correspond to orthogonality.
papers.key_findings:
Binary features can be represented as vectors in the transformed representation space, with words belonging to the feature having similar projections onto the vector.
Categorical concepts are represented as polytopes, where vertices correspond to vector representations of the concept's elements.
Hierarchical relationships (e.g., parent-child) are geometrically encoded as orthogonality between the corresponding vector representations.
Empirical validation on Gemma and LLaMA-3 models shows the estimated vector representations for WordNet concepts align with the semantic hierarchy, exhibiting the predicted orthogonal structure.
The canonical representation space (using a causal inner product) is necessary to observe the hierarchical orthogonality; it does not hold under the naive Euclidean inner product.
papers.limitation:
The analysis and whitening transformation are limited to the final layer representation; understanding the geometry of internal layers remains an open question.
Perfect linear representations as defined may not be found by gradient descent in practice; the theory assumes their existence.
future_direction: Extending the geometric analysis to the internal layers of language models.
Designing interpretability methods (e.g., sparse autoencoders) that explicitly account for the hierarchical structure of semantic concepts.
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis is the informal idea that semantic concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of large language models (LLMs). Previous work has shown how to make this notion precise for representing binary concepts that have natural contrasts (e.g., {male, female}) as directions in representation space. However, many natural concepts do not have natural contrasts (e.g., whether the output is about an animal). In this work, we show how to extend the formalization of the linear representation hypothesis to represent features (e.g., is_animal) as vectors. This allows us to immediately formalize the representation of categorical concepts as polytopes in the representation space. Further, we use the formalization to prove a relationship between the hierarchical structure of concepts and the geometry of their representations. We validate these theoretical results on the Gemma and LLaMA-3 large language models, estimating representations for 900+ hierarchically related concepts using data from WordNet.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: Using Artificial French Data to Understand the Emergence of Gender Bias in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether gender is ingrained in a word's representation or dynamically computed from context, and which characteristics of the training set affect an NLM's ability to capture gender information.
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models do not necessarily amplify gender imbalances in training data, and gender bias can emerge even with balanced data. Gender information can be ingrained in word representations or dynamically computed from context.
papers.conclusion: The findings challenge the assumption that training data imbalance is the sole cause of gender bias and suggest that transformers are not inherently biased to reproduce frequent patterns. Future work will generalize observations to natural language data.
papers.key_findings:
For words seen in gendered contexts during training, gender is ingrained in their representations, allowing correct assignment even in ambiguous contexts.
For words not seen in gendered contexts, the model can infer gender from context, but performance is near chance if only seen in ambiguous contexts.
For epicene nouns, the model accurately assigns gender based on context, but in ambiguous contexts, it tends to assign the most frequent gender from training.
Word frequency affects gender assignment in ambiguous contexts, with higher frequency leading to better accuracy.
Gender distribution in training data does not have a substantial impact on the degree of bias; models can exhibit bias even with balanced data.
papers.limitation:
The use of probes introduces an additional system rather than directly studying LM behavior.
The findings may not extrapolate to real models trained on natural language due to model size and data differences.
The PCFGs are based on French, and gender expression varies across languages.
The work considers a binary gender system.
future_direction: Generalizing observations to models trained on natural language data.
Exploring more intricate PCFGs to support coreference resolution challenges.
Examining how model and dataset sizes impact experiments.
papers.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated the ability of neural language models to learn various linguistic properties without direct supervision. This work takes an initial step towards exploring the less researched topic of how neural models discover linguistic properties of words, such as gender, as well as the rules governing their usage. We propose to use an artificial corpus generated by a PCFG based on French to precisely control the gender distribution in the training data and determine under which conditions a model correctly captures gender information or, on the contrary, appears gender-biased.

papers.title: A Practical Method for Generating String Counterfactuals
papers.research_question: How can representation space interventions in language models be converted into string-level counterfactuals to analyze linguistic changes and interpret encoded concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to generate string counterfactuals from representation space interventions in language models, allowing for the interpretation of linguistic alterations and the mitigation of bias through data augmentation.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a method for converting representation space interventions into string-level counterfactuals, bridging the gap between abstract manipulations and textual changes, and demonstrates its utility for bias analysis and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
String counterfactuals can be effectively generated from representation interventions, revealing gender biases in language models.
The counterfactuals show stereotypical word associations, such as increased profession-related words in male biographies.
Using these counterfactuals for data augmentation improves fairness in classification tasks without reducing accuracy.
Different intervention methods (LEACE, MiMiC, MiMiC+) produce varying linguistic changes and effectiveness.
Human evaluation confirms that interventions successfully alter perceived gender while maintaining text quality in most cases.
papers.limitation:
Quality of the inversion model may introduce imperfections and unwanted changes in the text.
Reliance on markers for gender rather than true causal factors due to the opacity of natural language generation.
Use of binary gender labels is a simplification of the complex, nonbinary construct of gender.
future_direction: Refine the inversion process to improve quality.
Extend the method to other interventions and concepts beyond binary gender.
Employ controlled synthetic settings to assess causal factors more accurately.
papers.abstract: Interventions targeting the representation space of language models (LMs) have emerged as an effective means to influence model behavior. Such methods are employed, for example, to eliminate or alter the encoding of demographic information such as gender within the model's representations and, in so doing, create a counterfactual representation. However, because the intervention operates within the representation space, understanding precisely what aspects of the text it modifies poses a challenge. In this paper, we give a method to convert representation counterfactuals into string counterfactuals. We demonstrate that this approach enables us to analyze the linguistic alterations corresponding to a given representation space intervention and to interpret the features utilized to encode a specific concept. Moreover, the resulting counterfactuals can be used to mitigate bias in classification through data augmentation.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What does 'linear representation' actually mean in the context of language models, and how can we make sense of geometric notions like cosine similarity and projection in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the linear representation hypothesis using counterfactuals, connects it to linear probing and model steering, and introduces a causal inner product that unifies different notions of linear representation and respects semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes linear representation and shows that all natural variants of this notion can be unified through a causal inner product, which plays a critical role in enabling interpretation and control of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts are represented as directions in the unembedding space, supporting the linear representation hypothesis.
The proposed causal inner product respects causal separability, making causally separable concepts approximately orthogonal.
The unembedding representation of a concept can be used as a linear probe to predict the concept from context embeddings.
The embedding representation (obtained via the causal inner product) can be used for intervention, steering the model's output towards a target concept.
The Euclidean inner product does not always capture semantic structure, while the causal inner product does.
papers.abstract: Informally, the 'linear representation hypothesis' is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity or projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of "linear representation", one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (sentence) space. We then prove these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

papers.title: Do LSTMs See Gender? Probing the Ability of LSTMs to Learn Abstract Syntactic Rules
papers.research_question: Does the LSTM learn abstract grammatical rules for gender agreement in French, or does it rely on simple heuristics like clues from gendered articles?
papers.core_contribution: LSTMs can perform long-distance gender agreement in French but show inaccuracies on plural phrases without gendered articles, suggesting reliance on surface clues rather than abstract syntactic rules.
papers.conclusion: Gender agreement is a useful probe for investigating LSTM's linguistic capabilities and the extent to which they learn abstract syntactic rules.
papers.key_findings:
LSTMs achieve high accuracy on gender agreement tasks even with long distractor phrases.
Performance varies more on shorter phrases with gender attractors, contrary to human behavior where longer phrases cause more errors.
Models may rely on gendered articles for agreement, as shown by lower accuracy on plural phrases where articles are uninformative.
Gender agreement accuracy is robust across different contexts like noun-adjective and noun-passive-verb agreement.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on short phrases with attractors deviates from human behavior, suggesting limitations in mimicking human language processing.
The study does not provide a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform gender agreement.
future_direction: Characterize the role of articles and other gender indicators in agreement.
Explore gender agreement in contexts beyond noun-predicate agreement.
Investigate whether learnt gender rules generalize to novel nouns.
papers.abstract: LSTMs trained on next-word prediction can accurately perform linguistic tasks that require tracking long-distance syntactic dependencies. Notably, model accuracy approaches human performance on number agreement tasks (Gulordava et al., 2018). However, we do not have a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform such linguistic tasks. Do LSTMs learn abstract grammatical rules, or do they rely on simple heuristics? Here, we test gender agreement in French which requires tracking both hierarchical syntactic structures and the inherent gender of lexical units. Our model is able to reliably predict long-distance gender agreement in two subject-predicate contexts: noun-adjective and noun-passive-verb agreement. The model showed more inaccuracies on plural noun phrases with gender attractors compared to singular cases, suggesting a reliance on clues from gendered articles for agreement. Overall, our study highlights key ways in which LSTMs deviate from human behaviour and questions whether LSTMs genuinely learn abstract syntactic rules and categories. We propose using gender agreement as a useful probe to investigate the underlying mechanisms, internal representations, and linguistic capabilities of LSTM language models.

papers.title: Monolingual and Multilingual Reduction of Gender Bias in Contextualized Representations
papers.research_question: How can we effectively reduce gender bias in contextualized representations using DensRay, and how is gender information distributed in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using DensRay to debias contextualized representations, showing it performs comparably to prior methods, is more robust, preserves language model performance better, and enables multilingual debiasing.
papers.conclusion: DensRay is an effective method for reducing gender bias in contextualized representations, maintaining model performance, and can be applied multilingually.
papers.key_findings:
DensRay effectively mitigates gender bias on OCCTMP and association tests.
DensRay preserves language model performance on Wikitext-2 and GLUE tasks better than other methods.
Gender information is spread across all attention heads and most layers in BERT, with no single head responsible.
DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on token and sentence levels.
DensRay can be used for zero-shot multilingual debiasing (e.g., debias Chinese using English data).
papers.limitation:
Token-level bias scores work well for monolingual BERT but not for multilingual BERT.
The method focuses only on the gender direction and may not address biases from implicitly gendered terms.
future_direction: Investigate multilingual transfer of debiasing techniques more closely.
Investigate debiasing with non-binary approaches (beyond male-female binary).
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) learn stereotypes held by humans and reflected in text from their training corpora, including gender bias. When PLMs are used for downstream tasks such as picking candidates for a job, people's lives can be negatively affected by these learned stereotypes. Prior work usually identifies a linear gender subspace and removes gender information by eliminating the subspace. Following this line of work, we propose to use DensRay, an analytical method for obtaining interpretable dense subspaces. We show that DensRay performs on-par with prior approaches, but provide arguments that it is more robust and provide indications that it preserves language model performance better. By applying DensRay to attention heads and layers of BERT we show that gender information is spread across all attention heads and most of the layers. Also we show that DensRay can obtain gender bias scores on both token and sentence levels. Finally, we demonstrate that we can remove bias multilingually, e.g., from Chinese, using only English training data.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: CausaLM: Causal Model Explanation Through Counterfactual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the true causal effect of a high-level concept (e.g., adjectives, topics, gender, race) on the predictions of a text classifier, distinguishing between correlation and causation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CausaLM, a framework that uses adversarial fine-tuning of language representation models (like BERT) to learn counterfactual representations, enabling estimation of the causal effect of a concept on a classifier's predictions without generating counterfactual text.
papers.conclusion: Causal model explanation is crucial for understanding and mitigating biases in NLP models, and CausaLM provides an effective framework for estimating causal effects of concepts on classifier predictions using counterfactual language representations.
papers.key_findings:
CausaLM can effectively estimate the causal effect of concepts (adjectives, topics, gender, race) on model predictions, outperforming correlation-based baselines.
The method can create language representations that are unaffected by a specific concept, which can be used to mitigate unwanted bias ingrained in the data.
The framework provides a way to answer causal questions about model behavior without requiring manually created counterfactual examples, relying only on observational data.
papers.limitation:
The method requires a causal graph and the choice of control concepts, which depends on the model of the world and may not capture all confounders.
Evaluation is conducted on specific, constructed concepts and datasets; real-world applications may involve more complex and numerous concepts.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex causal graphs and a wider range of concepts.
Applying the method to other modalities beyond text.
Developing richer, more complex datasets for evaluating causal estimators in more realistic settings.
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding predictions made by deep neural networks is notoriously difficult, but also crucial to their dissemination. As all machine learning–based methods, they are as good as their training data, and can also capture unwanted biases. While there are tools that can help understand whether such biases exist, they do not distinguish between correlation and causation, and might be ill-suited for text-based models and for reasoning about high level language concepts. A key problem of estimating the causal effect of a concept of interest on a given model is that this estimation requires the generation of counterfactual examples, which is challenging with existing generation technology. To bridge that gap, we propose CausaLM, a framework for producing causal model explanations using counterfactual language representation models. Our approach is based on fine-tuning of deep contextualized embedding models with auxiliary adversarial tasks derived from the causal graph of the problem. Concretely, we show that by carefully choosing auxiliary adversarial pre-training tasks, language representation models such as BERT can effectively learn a counterfactual representation for a given concept of interest, and be used to estimate its true causal effect on model performance. A byproduct of our method is a language representation model that is unaffected by the tested concept, which can be useful in mitigating unwanted bias ingrained in the data.

papers.title: Locating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the locations and generation mechanisms of gender bias in large language models, and how can it be mitigated effectively while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates locating and mitigating gender bias in a unified framework, using causal mediation analysis to trace bias to bottom MLP and top attention modules, and proposes the LSDM knowledge-editing method to effectively debias while preserving model capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias in LLMs is generated by the bottom MLP modules and extracted by top attention modules; the LSDM method effectively mitigates this bias while preserving model capabilities and can be extended to unseen occupational pronouns.
papers.key_findings:
The bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention modules acting on the final word are primary contributors to gender bias generation.
The proposed LSDM method reduces gender bias by an average of 71.4% across tested models and datasets.
LSDM outperforms fine-tuning and counterfactual data augmentation baselines in debiasing effectiveness and in preserving model performance on knowledge and reasoning tasks.
LSDM mitigates catastrophic forgetting, maintaining model capabilities on seven proficiency test datasets.
LSDM can generalize to reduce bias in some unseen neutral occupational pronouns, though effectiveness is reduced for out-of-distribution cases.
papers.limitation:
The collective influence of model components on the output has not been extensively studied.
LSDM's effectiveness remains poor for occupational pronouns outside the distribution.
The method focuses only on gender bias in occupational pronouns; extending to a broader range of biases is future work.
future_direction: Delve deeper into the mechanics of the debias method to thoroughly understand and apply it to enhance the model's knowledge performance.
Extend the method to a broader range of biases beyond gender and occupational pronouns.
papers.abstract: Large language models(LLM) are pre-trained on extensive corpora to learn facts and human cognition which contain human preferences. However, this process can inadvertently lead to these models acquiring biases and stereotypes prevalent in society. Prior research has typically tackled the issue of bias through a one-dimensional perspective, concentrating either on locating or mitigating it. This limited perspective has created obstacles in facilitating research on bias to synergistically complement and progressively build upon one another. In this study, we integrate the processes of locating and mitigating bias within a unified framework. Initially, we use causal mediation analysis to trace the causal effects of different components' activation within a large language model. Building on this, we propose the LSDM (Least Square Debias Method), a knowledge-editing based method for mitigating gender bias in occupational pronouns, and compare it against two baselines on three gender bias datasets and seven knowledge competency test datasets. The experimental results indicate that the primary contributors to gender bias are the bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention module acting on the final word in the sentence. Furthermore, LSDM mitigates gender bias in the model more effectively than the other baselines, while fully preserving the model's capabilities in all other aspects.

papers.title: More than Correlation: Do Large Language Models Learn Causal Representations of Space?
papers.research_question: Does the internal spatial representation in large language models have a causal effect on their behavior in geospatial tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models learn internal spatial representations of location words, and these representations causally influence the model's performance on geospatial tasks.
papers.conclusion: Through representational similarity analysis and probing, the paper shows that both DeBERTa-v2 and GPT-Neo learned spatial representations of location words, and intervention experiments demonstrate these representations have causal effects on model output.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden states of city names in DeBERTa and GPT-Neo correlate with real-world geospatial distances, as shown by representational similarity analysis.
Linear and non-linear probes can map hidden states to latitude and longitude with low error, indicating the presence of spatial information.
A novel GeoDist loss function, which accounts for spherical geometry, improves probing performance over mean squared error.
Causal intervention experiments show that aligning hidden states with true geographic coordinates improves accuracy in a country prediction task, while misaligning degrades it.
Perturbing hidden states with spatial information affects next-word prediction for country names, demonstrating causal use of spatial representations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to location words and geospatial tasks; it is unclear how spatial representations affect other types of words and non-geospatial tasks.
future_direction: Investigate spatial representations for words without inherent geographical property
Study the effect of spatial representation perturbation on tasks that do not rely on geographical knowledge
papers.abstract: Recent work found high mutual information between the learned representations of large language models (LLMs) and the geospatial property of its input, hinting an emergent internal model of space. However, whether this internal space model has any causal effects on the LLMs' behaviors was not answered by that work, led to criticism of these findings as mere statistical correlation. Our study focused on uncovering the causality of the spatial representations in LLMs. In particular, we discovered the potential spatial representations in DeBERTa, GPT-Neo using representational similarity analysis and linear and non-linear probing. Our casual intervention experiments showed that the spatial representations influenced the model's performance on next word prediction and a downstream task that relies on geospatial information. Our experiments suggested that the LLMs learn and use an internal model of space in solving geospatial related tasks.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
papers.research_question: How do multimodal large language models (MLLMs) balance memorized world knowledge priors and visual input when they conflict?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Visual CounterFact, a dataset of visual counterfactuals, and PvP steering vectors, a method to control whether MLLMs rely on visual input or memorized world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Provides a new framework for interpreting and controlling MLLMs, advancing the ability to understand and control the interaction between memory and perception.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts.
Model predictions shift from memorized priors to visual evidence in mid-to-late layers, revealing a competition between modalities.
PvP steering vectors can successfully shift model predictions from world knowledge to counterfactual answers with high success rates (e.g., 99.3% for color).
Steering vectors reshape internal attention mechanisms more effectively than prompt changes alone.
There is an asymmetry: steering from world knowledge to counterfactuals is easier than the reverse.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on three state-of-the-art models, which do not represent the full spectrum of multimodal architectures.
Steering models from visual perception back to world knowledge is more difficult than the reverse, suggesting an asymmetry.
future_direction: Expand analysis to a broader range of models to explore how architectural design impacts reliance on perception versus prior knowledge.
Further understand the asymmetry in how MLLMs prioritize in-context versus memorized information.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform well on tasks such as visual question answering, but it remains unclear whether their reasoning relies more on memorized world knowledge or on the visual information present in the input image. To investigate this, we introduce Visual CounterFact, a new dataset of visually-realistic counterfactuals that put world knowledge priors (e.g, red strawberry) into direct conflict with visual input (e.g, blue strawberry). Using Visual CounterFact, we show that model predictions initially reflect memorized priors, but shift toward visual evidence in mid-to-late layers. This dynamic reveals a competition between the two modalities, with visual input ultimately overriding priors during evaluation. To control this behavior, we propose Pixels Versus Priors (PvP) steering vectors, a mechanism for controlling model outputs toward either world knowledge or visual input through activation-level interventions. On average, PvP successfully shifts 99.3% of color and 80.8% of size predictions from priors to counterfactuals. Together, these findings offer new tools for interpreting and controlling factual behavior in multimodal models.

papers.title: How Language Models Prioritize Contextual Grammatical Cues?
papers.research_question: How do language models handle gender agreement when multiple valid gender cue words are present in the context, and which contextual cues do they prioritize?
papers.core_contribution: Encoder-based models (BERT) tend to prioritize the first cue in the context for gender agreement, while decoder-based models (GPT-2) rely more on the final cue.
papers.conclusion: Encoder-based and decoder-based Transformer language models behave differently in prioritizing contextual cues for gender agreement, with BERT relying on earlier cues and GPT-2 on later ones.
papers.key_findings:
BERT significantly incorporates earlier cue words into the representation of the target word, starting from the middle layers.
GPT-2 significantly attends to the later cue words in the context, starting from earlier layers and peaking near the final layer.
The predictions from context-mixing analysis and activation patching are consistent, indicating cues that contribute more to the target representation also play a crucial role in the final decision.
Fine-tuning intensifies the observed behaviors: BERT pays dominantly to the first cue, and GPT-2 increases the importance of the last cue.
The reliance on cue position is consistent even when the first cue is a pronoun instead of a name.
papers.limitation:
Experiments and findings are based on a grammatical agreement task as a well-defined scenario where multiple cues exist in a context.
Experiments were run on two widely used language models but with base size due to limited computational budget.
future_direction: Extend experiments to include more recent, large language models.
Explore other case studies, such as Question Answering datasets, where multiple cues in the context refer to the answer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have shown an excellent ability to effectively capture and utilize contextual information. Although various analysis techniques have been used to quantify and trace the contribution of single contextual cues to a target task such as subject-verb agreement or coreference resolution, scenarios in which multiple relevant cues are available in the context remain underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how language models handle gender agreement when multiple gender cue words are present, each capable of independently disambiguating a target gender pronoun. We analyze two widely used Transformer-based models: BERT, an encoder-based, and GPT-2, a decoder-based model. Our analysis employs two complementary approaches: context mixing analysis, which tracks information flow within the model, and a variant of activation patching, which measures the impact of cues on the model's prediction. We find that BERT tends to prioritize the first cue in the context to form both the target word representations and the model's prediction, while GPT-2 relies more on the final cue. Our findings reveal striking differences in how encoder-based and decoder-based models prioritize and use contextual information for their predictions.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Unsupervised Concept Vector Extraction for Bias Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we extract concept representations (like gender) from LLMs without labeled data and use them to measure and manipulate bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (WMD) for extracting concept steering vectors from LLMs and a projection-based intervention method for bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is effective for extracting steering vectors and mitigating bias in LLMs, and it generalizes to other protected attributes like race.
papers.key_findings:
The WMD method extracts steering vectors that have higher correlation with gender bias than the difference-in-means method.
The projection-based intervention effectively reduces gender bias in model predictions.
The method generalizes to racial bias.
Steering vectors can be transferred to different tasks (Winogenerated and occupational stereotypes).
Debiasing via steering does not significantly harm general model capabilities (MMLU and IFEVAL).
papers.limitation:
The approach oversimplifies gender as a binary concept and does not account for non-binary identities.
The method may not be applicable when factual gender information is needed in predictions.
future_direction: Expand evaluation to a broader range of tasks.
Adopt a more comprehensive approach that considers intersectionality of gender with other social identities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to perpetuate stereotypes and exhibit biases. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, but most work studies biases as a black-box problem without considering how concepts are represented within the model. We adapt techniques from representation engineering to study how the concept of "gender" is represented within LLMs. We introduce a new method that extracts concept representations via probability weighting without labeled data and efficiently selects a steering vector for measuring and manipulating the model's representation. We develop a projection-based method that enables precise steering of model predictions and demonstrate its effectiveness in mitigating gender bias in LLMs and show that it also generalizes to racial bias. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hannahxchen/gender-bias-steering

papers.title: Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax
papers.research_question: What is the causal effect of morpho-syntactic features like gender and number on contextualized representations in pre-trained models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a naturalistic causal probing framework using syntactic interventions to estimate causal effects of morpho-syntactic features, showing stable estimates and highlighting limitations of correlational probes.
papers.conclusion: The naturalistic causal probing framework enables accurate estimation of causal effects of morpho-syntactic features, revealing biases and limitations of correlational probes.
papers.key_findings:
Naturalistic causal probing provides stable average treatment effect (ATE) estimates for gender and number across different corpora.
ATE estimates from naturalistic data are more robust compared to naïve correlational estimators and template-based approaches.
Grammatical gender and number are encoded by a small number of principal axes in the contextualized representations of BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2.
RoBERTa exhibits gender bias, being more likely to predict certain adjectives for feminine or masculine nouns.
