This is usually done via a set of simple classification tasks, termed probes, to evaluate the information encoded in the embedding space. However, the involvement of a trainable classifier leads to entanglement between the probe's results and the classifier's nature. As a result, contemporary works on probing include tasks that do not involve training of auxiliary models. In this work we introduce the term indicator tasks for non-trainable tasks which are used to query embedding spaces for the existence of certain properties, and claim that this kind of tasks may point to a direction opposite to probes, and that this contradiction complicates the decision on whether a property exists in an embedding space. We demonstrate our claims with two test cases, one dealing with gender debiasing and another with the erasure of morphological information from embedding spaces. We show that the application of a suitable indicator provides a more accurate picture of the information captured and removed compared to probes. We thus conclude that indicator tasks should be implemented and taken into consideration when eliciting information from embedded representations.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts across modalities
papers.research_question: Do language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across different input modalities (text and images)?
papers.core_contribution: Language models predict brain activity better in regions with high semantic consistency across modalities, even when those regions are not language-selective, suggesting LMs develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.conclusion: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across modalities, indicating that LMs may internally develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.key_findings:
Brain regions with higher semantic consistency (responding similarly to concepts across text and image paradigms) are better predicted by LM representations.
This correlation holds even in brain regions with weak language selectivity.
Representational similarity between LMs and semantically consistent brain regions is significant and increases for vision-language models when using both text and image stimuli.
Both language-only and vision-language models show alignment with semantically consistent brain regions.
papers.limitation:
The picture paradigm correlation is lower and skewed by visual cortex areas that encode images but not necessarily concepts.
The study uses an inter-participant noise ceiling due to lack of repeated trials, which may not capture all variability.
papers.abstract: Cognitive science and neuroscience have long faced the challenge of disentangling representations of language from representations of conceptual meaning. As the same problem arises in today's language models (LMs), we investigate the relationship between LM--brain alignment and two neural metrics: (1) the level of brain activation during processing of sentences, targeting linguistic processing, and (2) a novel measure of meaning consistency across input modalities, which quantifies how consistently a brain region responds to the same concept across paradigms (sentence, word cloud, image) using an fMRI dataset (Pereira et al., 2018). Our experiments show that both language-only and language-vision models predict the signal better in more meaning-consistent areas of the brain, even when these areas are not strongly sensitive to language processing, suggesting that LMs might internally represent cross-modal conceptual meaning.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: Linear Spatial World Models Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly encode linear spatial world models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that large language models encode linear spatial world models, showing that spatial relations are represented in a low-dimensional subspace with geometric structure and are functionally used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that large language models do encode a basic spatial world model linearly within their representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes achieve near-perfect accuracy in decoding spatial relations, indicating linear encoding.
PCA reveals a low-dimensional subspace where spatial relations are organized geometrically (inverse relations are antipodal, orthogonal relations are perpendicular).
Spatial representations are compositional: composed relations correspond to vector sums of atomic relations.
Object positions are consistently represented in the same spatial subspace.
Causal interventions (activation steering) show that the spatial subspace is functionally used by the model for prediction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not investigate other essential components of a full world model, such as temporal dynamics or object permanence.
The analysis focuses on a limited set of spatial relations.
The generality of the findings to other model types remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to cover a broader and more diverse set of spatial directions.
Investigating other components of world models such as temporal dynamics.
Testing generalization to other model types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent abilities across diverse tasks, raising the question of whether they acquire internal world models. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode linear spatial world models, which we define as linear representations of physical space and object configurations. We introduce a formal framework for spatial world models and assess whether such structure emerges in contextual embeddings. Using a synthetic dataset of object positions, we train probes to decode object positions and evaluate geometric consistency of the underlying space. We further conduct causal interventions to test whether these spatial representations are functionally used by the model. Our results provide empirical evidence that LLMs encode linear spatial world models.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Local Contrastive Editing of Gender Stereotypes
papers.research_question: How can we localize individual weights that drive stereotypical gender bias in language models and modify these weights to steer and mitigate the bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces local contrastive editing, a two-step method to localize and edit a small subset (<0.5%) of model weights that encode gender bias, enabling flexible control and mitigation of bias while largely preserving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Stereotypical gender bias is encoded in specific subsets of weights within language models, and local contrastive editing can effectively identify and modify these subsets to control and mitigate bias.
papers.key_findings:
A very small subset (<0.5%) of model weights is responsible for encoding stereotypical gender bias.
Local contrastive editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) can successfully steer and mitigate gender bias in a controlled manner.
The identified bias-encoding weights are concentrated in higher layers of the transformer, particularly in the attention output dense layer.
Editing based on strategic localization is crucial; uninformed editing of random weights does not effectively change bias.
The method preserves the model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance, except for value-based pruning which degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted using a single model architecture (BERT) and a single type of bias (gender bias).
Computational constraints limit the scope of experiments, as iterative magnitude pruning requires substantial resources.
The study uses a binary specification of gender (male/female), which does not encompass the full gender spectrum.
future_direction: Explore application of local contrastive editing to other tasks and domains beyond gender bias.
papers.abstract: Stereotypical bias encoded in language models (LMs) poses a threat to safe language technology, yet our understanding of how bias manifests in the parameters of LMs remains incomplete. We introduce local contrastive editing that enables the localization and editing of a subset of weights in a target model in relation to a reference model. We deploy this approach to identify and modify subsets of weights that are associated with gender stereotypes in LMs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that local contrastive editing can precisely localize and control a small subset (< 0.5%) of weights that encode gender bias. Our work (i) advances our understanding of how stereotypical biases can manifest in the parameter space of LMs and (ii) opens up new avenues for developing parameter-efficient strategies for controlling model properties in a contrastive manner.

papers.title: Is This Just Fantasy? Language Model Representations Reflect Human Judgments of Event Plausibility
papers.research_question: How do language models internally represent modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable)? How do these representations develop, do they reflect human categorization behavior, and what interpretable features do they correspond to?
papers.core_contribution: Language models form linear representations (modal difference vectors) that distinguish between modal categories (probable, improbable, impossible, inconceivable). These vectors are more diagnostic than output probabilities, emerge in an intuitive order during training, and reflect fine-grained human categorization behavior and interpretable features like event likelihood and imageability.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn internal representations of modal categories that go beyond output probabilities. These representations develop in an intuitive order and capture nuanced aspects of human categorization, offering a novel way to study world models in LMs and potentially human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Modal difference vectors within LM hidden states reliably classify sentences by modal category, outperforming classification based on sentence probability.
Modal difference vectors develop in a consistent order: inconceivable vs. others emerges first, followed by probable vs. impossible, then probable vs. improbable, and finally improbable vs. impossible.
Projections of sentences onto modal difference vectors create a feature space that accurately models human participants' graded categorization judgments.
Projections along the impossible-inconceivable vector correlate selectively with human ratings of imageability and the presence of physical objects/places.
Preliminary steering experiments show that adding modal difference vectors to the residual stream during generation can influence the modal category of the generated text.
future_direction: Using modal difference vectors to test the intuitive theories about the world that LMs encode from text.
Using modal difference vectors to generate hypotheses about human representations of modal categories, such as the role of imagination in distinguishing impossible from inconceivable events.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are used for a diverse range of tasks, from question answering to writing fantastical stories. In order to reliably accomplish these tasks, LMs must be able to discern the modal category of a sentence (i.e., whether it describes something that is possible, impossible, completely nonsensical, etc.). However, recent studies have called into question the ability of LMs to categorize sentences according to modality (Michaelov et al., 2025; Kauf et al., 2023). In this work, we identify linear representations that discriminate between modal categories within a variety of LMs, or modal difference vectors. Analysis of modal difference vectors reveals that LMs have access to more reliable modal categorization judgments than previously reported. Furthermore, we find that modal difference vectors emerge in a consistent order as models become more competent (i.e., through training steps, layers, and parameter count). Notably, we find that modal difference vectors identified within LM activations can be used to model fine-grained human categorization behavior. This potentially provides a novel view into how human participants distinguish between modal categories, which we explore by correlating projections along modal difference vectors with human participants' ratings of interpretable features. In summary, we derive new insights into LM modal categorization using techniques from mechanistic interpretability, with the potential to inform our understanding of modal categorization in humans.

papers.title: A deep learning account of how language affects thought
papers.research_question: How can words shape meaning? Specifically, how do shared labels highlight commonalities between concepts and contrasting labels make differences apparent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that performing two prediction tasks (predicting meaning and label) requires a compromise in network representations, leading labels to affect semantic representations. This is demonstrated through simulations showing fine-grained labels cause differentiation and coarse-grained labels cause convergence in semantic space.
papers.conclusion: The DCNN model offers an account of how linguistic labels can shape meaning, showing that labels distort semantic representations to support labeling, with shared labels leading to convergence and contrasting labels leading to differentiation.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing pressure to correctly use fine-grained labels leads to semantic representations moving apart from one another to reduce label confusion.
Increasing pressure to correctly use coarse-grained labels leads to semantic representations of items sharing a label becoming more similar.
The semantic space becomes increasingly distorted (less aligned with a reference embedding space) as labeling pressure increases.
The model demonstrates that discriminative learning principles can scale to natural categories and labeling schemes using photographic stimuli.
The account provides a candidate mechanism for how differences in labeling schemes across languages could influence thought.
papers.limitation:
When labeling pressure became extreme at high β, the integrity of the semantic space itself was weakened, leading to a minor reversal in the distance ratio.
The lower network layers (perceptual front-end) were kept fixed during learning, which may not reflect potential changes in perceptual processing due to labeling.
future_direction: Future simulations could allow weights in lower network layers to change in response to error when learning new concepts or labels.
DCNN models can be useful in understanding concept and word learning in children during typical and atypical development.
Network architectures may diverge from those used here to better reflect implementational aspects of the brain, such as long-range recurrence.
papers.abstract: How can words shape meaning? Shared labels highlight commonalities between concepts whereas contrasting labels make differences apparent. To address such findings, we propose a deep learning account that spans perception to decision (i.e. labelling). The model takes photographs as input, transforms them to semantic representations through computations that parallel the ventral visual stream, and finally determines the appropriate linguistic label. The underlying theory is that minimising error on two prediction tasks (predicting the meaning and label of a stimulus) requires a compromise in the network's semantic representations. Thus, differences in label use, whether across languages or levels of expertise, manifest in differences in the semantic representations that support label discrimination. We confirm these predictions in simulations involving fine-grained and coarse-grained labels. We hope these and allied efforts which model perception, semantics, and labelling at scale will advance developmental and neurocomputational accounts of concept and language learning.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: When are Lemons Purple? The Concept Association Bias of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do vision-language models like CLIP struggle with tasks requiring fine-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA)? The paper investigates the Concept Association Bias (CAB) as a potential cause.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the Concept Association Bias (CAB) in vision-language models, showing that it is prevalent in contrastively trained models and that deeper cross-modal interaction through fine-tuning can mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Association Bias (CAB) exists in vision-language models, particularly those trained with contrastive losses, and reducing CAB can improve performance on tasks like VQA, highlighting a brittleness in contrastive objectives.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP and other vision-language models exhibit Concept Association Bias (CAB), where they treat input as a bag of concepts and fill in missing concepts crossmodally, leading to errors in tasks like color recognition.
CAB is especially prominent in models trained with contrastive losses (e.g., CLIP, BLIP-contrast), while models trained solely with autoregressive loss (e.g., OFA) show minimal or no CAB.
The strength of CAB predicts performance on VQA-v2: models with lower CAB scores achieve higher accuracy on VQA.
Adding a Transformer head for deeper modality interaction and fine-tuning on VQA reduces CAB and improves VQA performance.
Fine-tuning may not fundamentally solve the binding problem, as models still struggle with unnatural color-object pairs, suggesting that fine-tuning simply allows models to pick up real-world co-occurrences.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to color and part-whole attributes, and does not explore other object-attribute relationships such as material, shape, or texture.
future_direction: Explore the effect of CAB on other vision-language tasks beyond VQA, such as visual entailment.
Investigate other object-attribute relationships beyond color and part-whole.
Study other vision-language models that incorporate more extensive modality interactions (e.g., FLAVA, ALBEF).
papers.abstract: Large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP have shown impressive performance on zero-shot image classification and image-to-text retrieval. However, such performance does not realize in tasks that require a finer-grained correspondence between vision and language, such as Visual Question Answering (VQA). We investigate why this is the case, and report an interesting phenomenon of vision-language models, which we call the Concept Association Bias (CAB), as a potential cause of the difficulty of applying these models to VQA and similar tasks. We find that models with CAB tend to treat input as a bag of concepts and attempt to fill in the other missing concept crossmodally, leading to an unexpected zero-shot prediction. We demonstrate CAB by showing that CLIP’s zero-shot classification performance greatly suffers when there is a strong concept association between an object (e.g. eggplant) and an attribute (e.g. color purple). We also show that the strength of CAB predicts the performance on VQA. We observe that CAB is prevalent in vision-language models trained with contrastive losses, even when autoregressive losses are jointly employed. However, a model that solely relies on autoregressive loss seems to exhibit minimal or no signs of CAB.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: Meaning without reference in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, even without direct reference to the real world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, where meaning is derived from the relationships between internal representational states, rather than requiring reference to the real world.
papers.conclusion: LLMs likely already share the foundation of how human concepts get their meaning through conceptual role theory.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs likely capture important aspects of meaning through conceptual role, approximating human cognition.
Meaning arises from the interrelations between concepts, which LLMs can learn from text prediction.
Reference is not necessary for meaning; many meaningful concepts lack referents.
LLMs' internal geometries and trajectories approximate those of humans, supporting conceptual role theory.
Text provides clues to conceptual role because human conceptual roles generated the text.
papers.limitation: LLMs do not perfectly capture human concepts and lack aspects like reference, inference, better compositionality, and consistent abstract reasoning.
future_direction: Enrich the internal conceptual roles of LLMs to better reflect human structure, inference, and algorithmic sophistication.
Incorporate multimodal data and experience to improve meaning.
papers.abstract: The widespread success of large language models (LLMs) has been met with skepticism that they possess anything like human concepts or meanings. Contrary to claims that LLMs possess no meaning whatsoever, we argue that they likely capture important aspects of meaning, and moreover work in a way that approximates a compelling account of human cognition in which meaning arises from conceptual role. Because conceptual role is defined by the relationships between internal representational states, meaning cannot be determined from a model's architecture, training data, or objective function, but only by examination of how its internal states relate to each other. This approach may clarify why and how LLMs are so successful and suggest how they can be made more human-like.

papers.title: Number Representations in LLMs: A Computational Parallel to Human Perception
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) encode numerical values in a logarithmic-like structure, similar to the human mental number line hypothesis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode numerical values with structured, sublinear compression akin to the human logarithmic mental number line, a pattern detectable via unsupervised methods like PCA but often obscured by supervised linear probes like PLS.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode numerical values with structured compression similar to the human mental number line, but this sublinearity is only detectable through unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods like PCA that preserve geometric relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Numerical embeddings in LLMs exhibit higher explained variance and stronger monotonicity compared to random letter sequences, indicating a structured number line.
The Scaling Rate Index (β) reveals sublinear scaling (β < 1) in many models, showing compression where distances between numbers decrease as values increase.
PCA captures the underlying sublinear structure of numerical representations, while PLS, as a supervised linear probe, often misses this non-uniformity by optimizing for covariance with the target.
Layer-wise analysis shows that the sublinear encoding is consistent across layers, with the layer of highest explained variance also showing strong monotonicity.
In real-world tasks, birth year data shows systematic sublinear encoding, while population data is less structured due to context-dependence and approximate expressions.
papers.abstract: Humans are believed to perceive numbers on a logarithmic mental number line, where smaller values are represented with greater resolution than larger ones. This cognitive bias, supported by neuroscience and behavioral studies, suggests that numerical magnitudes are processed in a sublinear fashion rather than on a uniform linear scale. Inspired by this hypothesis, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit a similar logarithmic-like structure in their internal numerical representations. By analyzing how numerical values are encoded across different layers of LLMs, we apply dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and PLS followed by geometric regression to uncover latent structures in the learned embeddings. Our findings reveal that the model's numerical representations exhibit sublinear spacing, with distances between values aligning with a logarithmic scale. This suggests that LLMs, much like humans, may encode numbers in a compressed, non-uniform manner.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: What if This Modified That? Syntactic Interventions via Counterfactual Embeddings
papers.research_question: How faithfully do probes portray information that language models actually use, and do models leverage syntactic information in their embeddings for downstream prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a gradient-based technique to generate counterfactual embeddings using probes, and uses it to find evidence that a masked-word BERT model uses a distance-based representation of syntax, while a QA-finetuned BERT model does not.
papers.conclusion: The technique provides evidence for a causal link between a distance-based representation of syntax and the outputs of a masked-word model, but not for a QA-finetuned model, and suggests that probe design should be informed by causal evidence.
papers.key_findings:
A gradient-based method can generate counterfactual embeddings that change both probe and model outputs, allowing causal analysis of model reasoning.
Distance-based probes (especially multi-layer ones) generated counterfactuals that shifted the masked-word BERT model's predictions according to syntactic principles, suggesting it uses a distance-like representation of syntax.
Depth-based probes did not produce consistent changes in the masked-word model's outputs.
The BERT model fine-tuned for question answering showed no consistent effect from counterfactual embeddings, suggesting it may not use the syntactic information detected by the probes.
Multi-layered non-linear probes outperformed linear probes in generating effective counterfactuals, challenging the prior guidance that simpler probes are preferable.
future_direction: Developing new probes backed by causal evidence.
Developing more sophisticated counterfactual generation techniques.
papers.abstract: Neural language models exhibit impressive performance on a variety of tasks, but their internal reasoning may be difficult to understand. Prior art aims to uncover meaningful properties within model representations via probes, but it is unclear how faithfully such probes portray information that the models actually use. To overcome such limitations, we propose a technique, inspired by causal analysis, for generating counterfactual embeddings within models. In experiments testing our technique, we produce evidence that suggests some BERT-based models use a tree-distance-like representation of syntax in downstream prediction tasks.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Emergent Structures and Training Dynamics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What structures emerge from training large language models, and what internal representations of linguistic features do these networks learn?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys existing research on emergent structures and training dynamics in large language models, identifies gaps in the literature, and motivates future work that grounds the study of LLMs in an analysis of their changing internal structure during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by summarizing the surveyed research on network structure, linguistic feature learning, and explainability, and highlights the need for more work on training dynamics and emergent structures specifically in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic structures (syntax, semantics) are encoded in LLMs, but there is debate about the extent and nature of this encoding, with some studies suggesting models may rely more on local ordering statistics and content words than hierarchical syntax.
Multilingual models develop cross-lingual structures that enable transfer, but their performance is often inferior to monolingual models when sufficient resources are available.
Network structures such as branch specialization, weight banding, and clustering emerge in neural networks, but these have been studied more in computer vision than in NLP for language models.
Training dynamics research shows that models acquire linguistic knowledge early in training, with local syntactic information learned before long-distance dependencies.
Explainability methods like probing, saliency maps, and integrated gradients are surveyed as ways to connect internal network structure to function, though each has limitations.
papers.limitation: The survey is limited by the existing literature, which lacks sufficient research on emergent functional units and self-organization within large language models.
future_direction: Studying the training dynamics of linguistic structure learning across a variety of model scales and architectures.
Applying research on self-organization and emergent network structures (e.g., from computer vision) to large language models to identify language-specific functional units.
Further understanding the factors that enable learning language-independent representations in multilingual models, especially for transfer between less similar language pairs.
papers.abstract: Ryan Teehan, Miruna Clinciu, Oleg Serikov, Eliza Szczechla, Natasha Seelam, Shachar Mirkin, Aaron Gokaslan. Proceedings of BigScience Episode #5 -- Workshop on Challenges & Perspectives in Creating Large Language Models. 2022.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Characterizing the Role of Similarity in the Property Inferences of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models perform property inheritance, and what roles do taxonomic relations and categorical similarities play in this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Language models' property inheritance behavior is jointly explained by taxonomic relations and categorical similarity, and these features are entangled in the model's internal representations.
papers.conclusion: LMs perform property inheritance with sensitivity to both taxonomic relations and similarity, and these two factors are entangled in their internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show high taxonomic sensitivity in property inheritance, but also positive correlation with similarity between categories.
LMs are more likely to extend a property when categories are taxonomically related and highly similar.
Causal analysis reveals that the subspaces responsible for property inheritance reflect both taxonomic and similarity features.
Taxonomy and similarity are fundamentally entangled in LM representations, even when trained on unambiguous taxonomic data.
LMs exhibit graded property inheritance behavior similar to humans, influenced by similarity.
papers.limitation:
Alternative similarities could have been used, such as WordNet similarities or LM-derived similarities.
The study focuses only on concrete object noun concepts, not abstract or ad-hoc concepts.
The work does not engage with knowledge editing, which could be an interesting extension.
Property inheritance is only one type of inductive problem; broader generalization is not studied.
Similarity in inductive problems can be context-sensitive, which is not accounted for with nonce properties.
future_direction: Exploring other similarity measures and their correlation with property inheritance.
Extending the investigation to abstract and ad-hoc concepts.
Testing the entanglement of taxonomy and similarity in human property inheritance.
papers.abstract: Property inheritance -- a phenomenon where novel properties are projected from higher level categories (e.g., birds) to lower level ones (e.g., sparrows) -- provides a unique window into how humans organize and deploy conceptual knowledge. It is debated whether this ability arises due to explicitly stored taxonomic knowledge vs. simple computations of similarity between mental representations. How are these mechanistic hypotheses manifested in contemporary language models? In this work, we investigate how LMs perform property inheritance with behavioral and causal representational analysis experiments. We find that taxonomy and categorical similarities are not mutually exclusive in LMs' property inheritance behavior. That is, LMs are more likely to project novel properties from one category to the other when they are taxonomically related and at the same time, highly similar. Our findings provide insight into the conceptual structure of language models and may suggest new psycholinguistic experiments for human subjects.

papers.title: Counterfactual Divergence Singularity: A Theoretical Model of High-Similarity Instability and Micro-Counterfactual Drift in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the relationship between input similarity and output divergence in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations be formalized, and what explains the instability near high similarity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS), a theoretical framework that characterizes instability in large language models under micro-counterfactual perturbations, showing that divergence increases sharply as semantic similarity approaches unity.
papers.conclusion: The Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS) captures instability in LLMs under micro-counterfactual perturbations, reframing challenges like hallucination as manifestations of local non-smoothness in semantic manifolds, and suggests new evaluation paradigms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Divergence exhibits a hyperbolic blow-up as semantic similarity approaches 1.
Semantic curvature increases logarithmically in high-similarity regimes.
Embedding drift is minimal for high-similarity pairs, but divergence is high, indicating a contradiction.
LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth, leading to instability near the identity boundary.
The CDS phenomenon provides a geometric explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and hallucination.
papers.limitation:
Scale and computational constraints with only 200 micro-counterfactual pairs.
Dependency on a single paraphraser (FLAN-T5-Base).
Dependence on a single embedding model (SBERT MiniLM-L6-v2).
Absence of output-level probability divergence analysis.
Limited to English-language textual inputs.
Interpretational boundaries, not claiming CDS explains all hallucinations.
future_direction: Scaling to larger datasets (e.g., 2,000–20,000 pairs).
Testing with different paraphrasers and embedding models.
Including output-level probability divergence analysis.
Extending to other languages and multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable fluency and contextual sensitivity, yet their behaviour under minimal semantic perturbations remains poorly understood. In particular, near-identical paraphrastic inputs—expected to yield stable and equivalent responses—often produce disproportionately divergent generative behaviour. This paper introduces the <bold>Counterfactual Divergence Singularity (CDS)</bold> , a theoretical and empirical framework that characterizes a previously underexplored instability regime in transformer-based language models. This work formalizes micro-counterfactual perturbations as infinitesimal semantic variations in embedding space and show that, as semantic similarity approaches unity, divergence metrics exhibit a hyperbolic blow-up. Using a controlled experimental pipeline based on FLAN-T5-generated paraphrases and Sentence-BERT semantic embeddings, this paper empirically demonstrate that divergence, curvature, and embedding drift collectively reveal a singular boundary where semantic proximity no longer guarantees behavioural stability. Despite minimal embedding displacement and near-maximal cosine similarity, reciprocal divergence measures increase sharply, exposing a structural nonlinearity in the input–output mapping of LLMs. The results suggest that LLM semantic manifolds are locally non-smooth and that standard embedding-based similarity metrics fail to capture instability near the identity boundary. This phenomenon provides a geometric and mathematical explanation for prompt sensitivity, counterfactual failure, and certain forms of hallucination observed in generative systems. By reframing these behaviours as consequences of latent-space singularities rather than isolated decoding artifacts, this work contributes a novel theoretical lens for evaluating robustness, interpretability, and reliability in large language models.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Images Speak Louder than Words: Understanding and Mitigating Bias in Vision-Language Model from a Causal Mediation Perspective
papers.research_question: How is bias generated and propagated within vision-language models, and which model components contribute most to it?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework using causal mediation analysis to measure and understand bias pathways in VLMs, finding image features are the primary contributor to gender bias, and demonstrates an effective mitigation strategy by blurring gender representations in the image encoder.
papers.conclusion: The introduced framework provides a way to measure, understand, and mitigate bias in VLMs, with image features identified as the primary contributor to bias, and targeting the image encoder for mitigation is effective.
papers.key_findings:
Image features contribute significantly more to model bias than text features, accounting for approximately 33% and 13% of bias in MSCOCO and PASCAL-SENTENCE datasets, respectively.
The image encoder's contribution to bias surpasses that of the text encoder and deep fusion encoder.
Contributions to bias from language and vision modalities are aligned and non-conflicting.
Blurring gender representations in the image encoder reduces bias by approximately 22.03% and 9.04% on MSCOCO and PASCAL-SENTENCE datasets, with minimal performance loss.
The deep fusion process, where image and text features interact, accounts for about 56% of the bias contributions from the encoders.
papers.limitation: The framework is primarily applicable to white-box models, as it requires interventions within the model's internal components.
future_direction: Expanding the framework to encompass additional modalities such as audio or video.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) pre-trained on extensive datasets can inadvertently learn biases by correlating gender information with specific objects or scenarios.
