A novel GeoDist loss function, which accounts for spherical geometry, improves probing performance over mean squared error.
Causal intervention experiments show that aligning hidden states with true geographic coordinates improves accuracy in a country prediction task, while misaligning degrades it.
Perturbing hidden states with spatial information affects next-word prediction for country names, demonstrating causal use of spatial representations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to location words and geospatial tasks; it is unclear how spatial representations affect other types of words and non-geospatial tasks.
future_direction: Investigate spatial representations for words without inherent geographical property
Study the effect of spatial representation perturbation on tasks that do not rely on geographical knowledge
papers.abstract: Recent work found high mutual information between the learned representations of large language models (LLMs) and the geospatial property of its input, hinting an emergent internal model of space. However, whether this internal space model has any causal effects on the LLMs' behaviors was not answered by that work, led to criticism of these findings as mere statistical correlation. Our study focused on uncovering the causality of the spatial representations in LLMs. In particular, we discovered the potential spatial representations in DeBERTa, GPT-Neo using representational similarity analysis and linear and non-linear probing. Our casual intervention experiments showed that the spatial representations influenced the model's performance on next word prediction and a downstream task that relies on geospatial information. Our experiments suggested that the LLMs learn and use an internal model of space in solving geospatial related tasks.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
papers.research_question: How do multimodal large language models (MLLMs) balance memorized world knowledge priors and visual input when they conflict?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Visual CounterFact, a dataset of visual counterfactuals, and PvP steering vectors, a method to control whether MLLMs rely on visual input or memorized world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Provides a new framework for interpreting and controlling MLLMs, advancing the ability to understand and control the interaction between memory and perception.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts.
Model predictions shift from memorized priors to visual evidence in mid-to-late layers, revealing a competition between modalities.
PvP steering vectors can successfully shift model predictions from world knowledge to counterfactual answers with high success rates (e.g., 99.3% for color).
Steering vectors reshape internal attention mechanisms more effectively than prompt changes alone.
There is an asymmetry: steering from world knowledge to counterfactuals is easier than the reverse.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on three state-of-the-art models, which do not represent the full spectrum of multimodal architectures.
Steering models from visual perception back to world knowledge is more difficult than the reverse, suggesting an asymmetry.
future_direction: Expand analysis to a broader range of models to explore how architectural design impacts reliance on perception versus prior knowledge.
Further understand the asymmetry in how MLLMs prioritize in-context versus memorized information.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform well on tasks such as visual question answering, but it remains unclear whether their reasoning relies more on memorized world knowledge or on the visual information present in the input image. To investigate this, we introduce Visual CounterFact, a new dataset of visually-realistic counterfactuals that put world knowledge priors (e.g, red strawberry) into direct conflict with visual input (e.g, blue strawberry). Using Visual CounterFact, we show that model predictions initially reflect memorized priors, but shift toward visual evidence in mid-to-late layers. This dynamic reveals a competition between the two modalities, with visual input ultimately overriding priors during evaluation. To control this behavior, we propose Pixels Versus Priors (PvP) steering vectors, a mechanism for controlling model outputs toward either world knowledge or visual input through activation-level interventions. On average, PvP successfully shifts 99.3% of color and 80.8% of size predictions from priors to counterfactuals. Together, these findings offer new tools for interpreting and controlling factual behavior in multimodal models.

papers.title: How Language Models Prioritize Contextual Grammatical Cues?
papers.research_question: How do language models handle gender agreement when multiple valid gender cue words are present in the context, and which contextual cues do they prioritize?
papers.core_contribution: Encoder-based models (BERT) tend to prioritize the first cue in the context for gender agreement, while decoder-based models (GPT-2) rely more on the final cue.
papers.conclusion: Encoder-based and decoder-based Transformer language models behave differently in prioritizing contextual cues for gender agreement, with BERT relying on earlier cues and GPT-2 on later ones.
papers.key_findings:
BERT significantly incorporates earlier cue words into the representation of the target word, starting from the middle layers.
GPT-2 significantly attends to the later cue words in the context, starting from earlier layers and peaking near the final layer.
The predictions from context-mixing analysis and activation patching are consistent, indicating cues that contribute more to the target representation also play a crucial role in the final decision.
Fine-tuning intensifies the observed behaviors: BERT pays dominantly to the first cue, and GPT-2 increases the importance of the last cue.
The reliance on cue position is consistent even when the first cue is a pronoun instead of a name.
papers.limitation:
Experiments and findings are based on a grammatical agreement task as a well-defined scenario where multiple cues exist in a context.
Experiments were run on two widely used language models but with base size due to limited computational budget.
future_direction: Extend experiments to include more recent, large language models.
Explore other case studies, such as Question Answering datasets, where multiple cues in the context refer to the answer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have shown an excellent ability to effectively capture and utilize contextual information. Although various analysis techniques have been used to quantify and trace the contribution of single contextual cues to a target task such as subject-verb agreement or coreference resolution, scenarios in which multiple relevant cues are available in the context remain underexplored. In this paper, we investigate how language models handle gender agreement when multiple gender cue words are present, each capable of independently disambiguating a target gender pronoun. We analyze two widely used Transformer-based models: BERT, an encoder-based, and GPT-2, a decoder-based model. Our analysis employs two complementary approaches: context mixing analysis, which tracks information flow within the model, and a variant of activation patching, which measures the impact of cues on the model's prediction. We find that BERT tends to prioritize the first cue in the context to form both the target word representations and the model's prediction, while GPT-2 relies more on the final cue. Our findings reveal striking differences in how encoder-based and decoder-based models prioritize and use contextual information for their predictions.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Unsupervised Concept Vector Extraction for Bias Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we extract concept representations (like gender) from LLMs without labeled data and use them to measure and manipulate bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (WMD) for extracting concept steering vectors from LLMs and a projection-based intervention method for bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is effective for extracting steering vectors and mitigating bias in LLMs, and it generalizes to other protected attributes like race.
papers.key_findings:
The WMD method extracts steering vectors that have higher correlation with gender bias than the difference-in-means method.
The projection-based intervention effectively reduces gender bias in model predictions.
The method generalizes to racial bias.
Steering vectors can be transferred to different tasks (Winogenerated and occupational stereotypes).
Debiasing via steering does not significantly harm general model capabilities (MMLU and IFEVAL).
papers.limitation:
The approach oversimplifies gender as a binary concept and does not account for non-binary identities.
The method may not be applicable when factual gender information is needed in predictions.
future_direction: Expand evaluation to a broader range of tasks.
Adopt a more comprehensive approach that considers intersectionality of gender with other social identities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to perpetuate stereotypes and exhibit biases. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, but most work studies biases as a black-box problem without considering how concepts are represented within the model. We adapt techniques from representation engineering to study how the concept of "gender" is represented within LLMs. We introduce a new method that extracts concept representations via probability weighting without labeled data and efficiently selects a steering vector for measuring and manipulating the model's representation. We develop a projection-based method that enables precise steering of model predictions and demonstrate its effectiveness in mitigating gender bias in LLMs and show that it also generalizes to racial bias. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hannahxchen/gender-bias-steering

papers.title: Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax
papers.research_question: What is the causal effect of morpho-syntactic features like gender and number on contextualized representations in pre-trained models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a naturalistic causal probing framework using syntactic interventions to estimate causal effects of morpho-syntactic features, showing stable estimates and highlighting limitations of correlational probes.
papers.conclusion: The naturalistic causal probing framework enables accurate estimation of causal effects of morpho-syntactic features, revealing biases and limitations of correlational probes.
papers.key_findings:
Naturalistic causal probing provides stable average treatment effect (ATE) estimates for gender and number across different corpora.
ATE estimates from naturalistic data are more robust compared to naïve correlational estimators and template-based approaches.
Grammatical gender and number are encoded by a small number of principal axes in the contextualized representations of BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2.
RoBERTa exhibits gender bias, being more likely to predict certain adjectives for feminine or masculine nouns.
Correlational probes perform well on original data but drop to near chance on counterfactually augmented data, indicating overestimation of property encoding.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a binary notion of gender, not representative of the full gender spectrum.
The heuristic intervention algorithm may make errors, though assumed acceptable.
future_direction: Improving the heuristic intervention algorithm to reduce errors.
papers.abstract: Probing has become a go-to methodology for interpreting and analyzing deep neural models in natural language processing. However, there is still a lack of understanding of the limitations and weaknesses of various types of probes. In this work, we suggest a strategy for input-level intervention on naturalistic sentences. Using our approach, we intervene on the morpho-syntactic features of a sentence, while keeping the rest of the sentence unchanged. Such an intervention allows us to causally probe pre-trained models. We apply our naturalistic causal probing framework to analyze the effects of grammatical gender and number on contextualized representations extracted from three pre-trained models in Spanish: the multilingual versions of BERT, RoBERTa, and GPT-2. Our experiments suggest that naturalistic interventions lead to stable estimates of the causal effects of various linguistic properties. Moreover, our experiments demonstrate the importance of naturalistic causal probing when analyzing pre-trained models.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Identifying and Adapting Transformer-Components Responsible for Gender Bias in an English Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we identify transformer components causally responsible for gender bias in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning of these components mitigate bias while preserving general language modeling performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffMask+, an efficient method for identifying transformer components causally responsible for gender bias, and demonstrates that targeted fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias with minimal degradation in general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that causal methods can identify components responsible for gender bias, and that parameter-efficient fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias with minimal harm to language modeling capabilities, though it underscores challenges in defining and measuring bias.
papers.key_findings:
The three causal discovery methods (CMA, ACDC, DiffMask+) identify largely overlapping sets of attention heads, primarily located in the last four layers of GPT-2 small.
Targeted fine-tuning of the identified attention heads reduces gender bias on the CrowS-Pairs and Professions datasets.
Fine-tuning only the identified heads preserves general language modeling performance (perplexity and BLiMP scores) better than full model fine-tuning or fine-tuning broader sets of components.
The dataset used for component discovery influences which components are identified, highlighting the sensitivity of causal methods to dataset choice.
DiffMask+ is computationally more efficient than automated circuit discovery (ACDC) while achieving similar results.
papers.limitation:
Operationalizing gender bias using minimal pairs of contrasting sentences simplifies gender as a binary construct and may not generalize well to other languages.
Causal discovery procedures are sensitive to the choice of dataset, which can affect the components identified.
future_direction: Develop more reliable and validated bias measures.
More attention to dataset development for bias analysis.
Extend mitigation strategies to other types of bias.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit and amplify many types of undesirable biases learned from the training data, including gender bias. However, we lack tools for effectively and efficiently changing this behavior without hurting general language modeling performance. In this paper, we study three methods for identifying causal relations between LM components and particular output: causal mediation analysis, automated circuit discovery and our novel, efficient method called DiffMask+ based on differential masking. We apply the methods to GPT-2 small and the problem of gender bias, and use the discovered sets of components to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning for bias mitigation. Our results show significant overlap in the identified components (despite huge differences in the computational requirements of the methods) as well as success in mitigating gender bias, with less damage to general language modeling compared to full model fine-tuning. However, our work also underscores the difficulty of defining and measuring bias, and the sensitivity of causal discovery procedures to dataset choice. We hope our work can contribute to more attention for dataset development, and lead to more effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.

papers.title: Verb Conjugation in Transformers Is Determined by Linear Encodings of Subject Number
papers.research_question: Does BERT use a linear encoding of subject number for verb conjugation, and how is this encoding distributed across layers and positions?
papers.core_contribution: BERT's verb conjugation relies on a linear encoding of subject number that can be manipulated to predictably affect accuracy, demonstrating interpretable representations in transformers.
papers.conclusion: BERT uses a linear encoding of subject number for verb conjugation, which is interpretable and can be causally manipulated, offering an example of linear feature representation in language models.
papers.key_findings:
Subject number is linearly encoded in BERT's hidden representations, and intervention can reverse conjugation accuracy.
The encoding originates in the subject position at early layers and moves to the verb position at later layers.
With redundant cues to subject number, the encoding distributes across multiple positions at middle layers.
Intervention has minimal side effects on number-neutral words, showing selectivity of the encoding.
Results are consistent across different BERT model instances.
papers.limitation:
Experimental control using a uniform syntactic template may not generalize to naturalistic settings where other factors influence verb conjugation.
Cannot prove that BERT does not use linear encodings for features where intervention fails, due to limitations of the INLP method.
future_direction: Investigating what other features may have linear encodings that can be similarly manipulated with causal intervention.
papers.abstract: Deep architectures such as Transformers are sometimes criticized for having uninterpretable "black-box" representations. We use causal intervention analysis to show that, in fact, some linguistic features are represented in a linear, interpretable format. Specifically, we show that BERT's ability to conjugate verbs relies on a linear encoding of subject number that can be manipulated with predictable effects on conjugation accuracy. This encoding is found in the subject position at the first layer and the verb position at the last layer, but distributed across positions at middle layers, particularly when there are multiple cues to subject number.

papers.title: MarIA and BETO are sexist: evaluating gender bias in large language models for Spanish
papers.research_question: How can gender bias be evaluated in Spanish masked language models, and to what extent is it present in popular pretrained models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an evaluation framework for gender bias in Spanish masked language models and finds varying levels of bias, with body-related adjectives more associated with women and behavior-related adjectives with men.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias is evident in Spanish language models, and the proposed evaluation framework provides interpretable metrics to measure it, which is crucial for deploying fair models in real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is present in all evaluated Spanish language models.
Bias is most pronounced in body-related adjectives for female templates and behavior-related adjectives for male templates.
The proposed metrics (BPI and BRI) effectively quantify bias across different adjective categorization schemes.
Models like BETO and MarIA show strong bias, while some BERTIN variants are less biased.
The framework is extensible to other protected attributes and languages.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other biases such as ethnicity, religion, or socio-economic status.
Apply the models to other tasks like text generation or sentiment prediction to study bias propagation.
Research methods to mitigate the identified bias in Spanish models.
papers.abstract: Abstract The study of bias in language models is a growing area of work, however, both research and resources are focused on English. In this paper, we make a first approach focusing on gender bias in some freely available Spanish language models trained using popular deep neural networks, like BERT or RoBERTa. Some of these models are known for achieving state-of-the-art results on downstream tasks. These promising results have promoted such models' integration in many real-world applications and production environments, which could be detrimental to people affected for those systems. This work proposes an evaluation framework to identify gender bias in masked language models, with explainability in mind to ease the interpretation of the evaluation results. We have evaluated 20 different models for Spanish, including some of the most popular pretrained ones in the research community. Our findings state that varying levels of gender bias are present across these models. This approach compares the adjectives proposed by the model for a set of templates. We classify the given adjectives into understandable categories and compute two new metrics from model predictions, one based on the internal state (probability) and the other one on the external state (rank). Those metrics are used to reveal biased models according to the given categories and quantify the degree of bias of the models under study.

papers.title: Language Models as Models of Language
papers.research_question: What can modern language models contribute to theoretical linguistics, particularly regarding language acquisition and competence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models, when trained on developmentally plausible data and tested with controlled experiments, can serve as testbeds for evaluating linguistic hypotheses and inform debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.conclusion: Closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure from exposure to data.
Language models exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even with developmentally plausible amounts of data.
Language models have inductive biases that favor natural language structures over impossible languages.
Language models can be used to test learnability claims and challenge strong nativist positions.
Causal intervention methods can help uncover the mechanisms by which language models process syntax.
papers.limitation: There is a large discrepancy between the amount of data used to train state-of-the-art language models and the data available to children during language acquisition.
future_direction: Using language models trained on developmentally plausible data (e.g., the BabyLM challenge).
Employing causal intervention methods to better understand model mechanisms.
Fostering closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers.
papers.abstract: This chapter critically examines the potential contributions of modern language models to theoretical linguistics. Despite their focus on engineering goals, these models' ability to acquire sophisticated linguistic knowledge from mere exposure to data warrants a careful reassessment of their relevance to linguistic theory. I review a growing body of empirical evidence suggesting that language models can learn hierarchical syntactic structure and exhibit sensitivity to various linguistic phenomena, even when trained on developmentally plausible amounts of data. While the competence/performance distinction has been invoked to dismiss the relevance of such models to linguistic theory, I argue that this assessment may be premature. By carefully controlling learning conditions and making use of causal intervention methods, experiments with language models can potentially constrain hypotheses about language acquisition and competence. I conclude that closer collaboration between theoretical linguists and computational researchers could yield valuable insights, particularly in advancing debates about linguistic nativism.

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause Representations on Agreement Prediction
papers.research_question: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlterRep, an intervention-based method to test if language models use linguistic features consistently with grammar, and finds that BERT models use relative clause boundary information in a grammatically consistent way, with some abstraction across RC types.
papers.conclusion: AlterRep provides a causal intervention method to test whether language models use linguistic information consistently with grammar, showing that BERT models use relative clause boundary information in a manner consistent with English grammar and that this representation is abstract across RC types.
papers.key_findings:
Counterfactual intervention in the middle layers of BERT-base modulates agreement error rate in RC sentences with attractors, increasing error when the verb is made to appear inside the RC and decreasing error when made to appear outside.
Only the information encoded in the middle layers (layers 5-8 in BERT-base) causally influences agreement behavior, despite all layers encoding RC boundary information, highlighting a dissociation between correlational and causal methods.
Interventions on RC boundary representations generalize across different RC types, suggesting that BERT encodes RC boundaries as an abstract linguistic category.
Interventions do not affect agreement predictions in sentences without attractors or without RCs, indicating specificity to contexts where RC boundaries are relevant.
Qualitatively similar causal effects are observed in other BERT variants (large, medium, small, mini), but not in BERT-tiny.
papers.limitation: AlterRep interventions are based on linear classifiers to identify concept subspaces in non-linear networks, so while positive results indicate causal effect, negative results should be interpreted more cautiously.
future_direction: Apply AlterRep to test linguistically motivated hypotheses about a wide range of structures and tasks, such as the role of semantic roles in natural language inference.
papers.abstract: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation. By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.

papers.title: What Triggers my Model? Contrastive Explanations Inform Gender Choices by Translation Models
papers.research_question: How to measure attribution levels of source words on machine translation model's gender decisions, which source words are most salient, and to what extent salient words agree with human perceptions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how contrastive explanations and saliency attribution can be used to understand gender bias in machine translation models, showing high overlap between model-attributed salient words and human annotations, with differences in part-of-speech categories and dependency distances.
papers.conclusion: The study moves beyond measuring bias to exploring its origins by comparing model and human perceptions, highlighting the importance of understanding model behavior for mitigating gender bias in machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
High overlap between model salient words and human annotations, with the best overlap achieved at the top 15% relative attribution threshold.
Nouns and verbs are the most salient part-of-speech categories for the model's gender decisions.
Salient words for the model are typically at a closer dependency distance to the target referent compared to human annotations.
The model predominantly translates gender-ambiguous referents into masculine forms, while human annotations show more variation.
Different approaches to measuring attribution levels yield varying overlaps, with relative attribution scores performing best.
papers.limitation:
The dataset comprising 60 sentences is very small.
Only one model (OPUS-MT) and two language pairs (EN→DE/ES) were tested.
Model tokenization impacts saliency analysis, and subword merging may introduce errors.
There is low inter-annotator agreement in human annotations, indicating variability in human perceptions.
The study focuses on binary gender, excluding non-binary or inclusive translations.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a larger dataset once available.
Compare different models and languages in future work.
Address the limitation of available open-source models and toolkits for contrastive approaches.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can be implemented as a means to understand decisions taken by (black box) models, such as machine translation (MT) or large language models (LLMs). Yet, research in this area has been limited in relation to a manifested problem in these models: gender bias. With this research, we aim to move away from simply measuring bias to exploring its origins. Working with gender-ambiguous natural source data, this study examines which context, in the form of input tokens in the source sentence, influences (or triggers) the translation model choice of a certain gender inflection in the target language. To analyse this, we use contrastive explanations and compute saliency attribution. We first address the challenge of a lacking scoring threshold and specifically examine different attribution levels of source words on the model gender decisions in the translation. We compare salient source words with human perceptions of gender and demonstrate a noticeable overlap between human perceptions and model attribution. Additionally, we provide a linguistic analysis of salient words. Our work showcases the relevance of understanding model translation decisions in terms of gender, how this compares to human decisions and that this information should be leveraged to mitigate gender bias.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: Voice, Bias, and Coreference: An Interpretability Study of Gender in Speech Translation
papers.research_question: How do speech translation models assign gender to speaker-referring terms, considering the influence of training data patterns, internal language model biases, and acoustic information from input audio?
papers.core_contribution: Speech translation models assign gender to speaker-referring terms by learning broader masculine biases from training data and using first-person pronouns to access acoustic gender cues distributed across formant frequencies, rather than relying solely on pitch.
papers.conclusion: ST models learn broad masculine biases and use first-person pronouns to access acoustic gender cues from formant frequencies, demonstrating distinct mechanisms for gender disambiguation in speech translation.
papers.key_findings:
Models do not memorize term-specific gender associations from training data but internalize a general masculine skew.
The internal language model (ILM) exhibits strong masculine bias, but acoustic input can override these preferences.
Contrastive feature attribution reveals that models rely on first-person pronouns like 'I' to link gendered terms back to the speaker.
Acoustic cues for gender assignment are distributed across the frequency spectrum, with emphasis on first and second formants, not concentrated in pitch.
There is an asymmetry: feminine predictions rely more on acoustic cues, while masculine predictions rely more on internal biases.
papers.limitation: The analysis uses a binary gender framework, excluding gender non-conforming individuals.
papers.abstract: Unlike text, speech conveys information about the speaker, such as gender, through acoustic cues like pitch. This gives rise to modality-specific bias concerns. For example, in speech translation (ST), when translating from languages with notional gender, such as English, into languages where gender-ambiguous terms referring to the speaker are assigned grammatical gender, the speaker's vocal characteristics may play a role in gender assignment. This risks misgendering speakers, whether through masculine defaults or vocal-based assumptions. Yet, how ST models make these decisions remains poorly understood. We investigate the mechanisms ST models use to assign gender to speaker-referring terms across three language pairs (en-es/fr/it), examining how training data patterns, internal language model (ILM) biases, and acoustic information interact. We find that models do not simply replicate term-specific gender associations from training data, but learn broader patterns of masculine prevalence. While the ILM exhibits strong masculine bias, models can override these preferences based on acoustic input. Using contrastive feature attribution on spectrograms, we reveal that the model with higher gender accuracy relies on a previously unknown mechanism: using first-person pronouns to link gendered terms back to the speaker, accessing gender information distributed across the frequency spectrum rather than concentrated in pitch.

papers.title: Color in Visual-Language Models: CLIP Deficiencies
papers.research_question: How is color encoded in CLIP, and what are the main deficiencies in its color labeling capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies deficiencies in CLIP's color encoding, including bias against achromatic colors and text prioritization, and analyzes neuron-level representations to explain these issues.
papers.conclusion: CLIP's color deficiencies may stem from training data biases, and progressive training could improve color representation.
papers.key_findings:
Achromatic stimuli are poorly related to the color concept, leading to errors in assigning black, white, or grey labels.
CLIP prioritizes text over visual information, exhibiting a strong Stroop effect where it reads color names instead of perceiving font color.
In global color assignments, CLIP labels the predominant color, except when it is achromatic.
CLIP can attribute color labels to specific image parts when instructed, but fails if the part is achromatic.
Color multi-modal neurons are found in shallow layers of CLIP, which may underlie color understanding.
papers.limitation: The black-box nature of models makes it hard to explain behavior
future_direction: Progressive training to ensure learning from basic to complex concepts
papers.abstract: This work explores how color is encoded in CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) which is currently the most influential VML (Visual Language model) in Artificial Intelligence. After performing different experiments on synthetic datasets created for this task, we conclude that CLIP is able to attribute correct color labels to colored visual stimulus, but, we come across two main deficiencies: (a) a clear bias on achromatic stimuli that are poorly related to the color concept, thus white, gray and black are rarely assigned as color labels; and (b) the tendency to prioritize text over other visual information. Here we prove it is highly significant in color labelling through an exhaustive Stroop-effect test. With the aim to find the causes of these color deficiencies, we analyse the internal representation at the neuron level. We conclude that CLIP presents an important amount of neurons selective to text, specially in deepest layers of the network, and a smaller amount of multi-modal color neurons which could be the key of understanding the concept of color properly. Our investigation underscores the necessity of refining color representation mechanisms in neural networks to foster a more comprehensive comprehension of colors as humans understand them, thereby advancing the efficacy and versatility of multimodal models like CLIP in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause\n Representations on Agreement Prediction
papers.research_question: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AlterRep, a counterfactual intervention method to test if language models use linguistic features consistently with grammar, and finds that BERT uses relative clause boundary information grammatically and abstractly.
papers.conclusion: AlterRep provides a way to test causal use of linguistic features in models, and shows BERT uses relative clause boundaries grammatically and abstractly.
papers.key_findings:
Only middle layers of BERT causally influence agreement prediction in a manner consistent with English grammar, while all layers encode RC boundary information.
RC boundary representations partially generalize across different RC types, suggesting abstract representation.
Interventions using random subspaces do not yield interpretable changes, indicating specificity of RC subspaces.
Similar patterns observed in BERT variants of different sizes, except BERT-tiny.
papers.limitation: AlterRep uses linear subspaces to analyze non-linear networks, so negative results may not be conclusive.
future_direction: Apply AlterRep to test hypotheses about a wide range of linguistic structures and tasks.
papers.abstract:
When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use
their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar
of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address
this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep
generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is
encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation.
By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these
counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can
draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question
on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of
different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use
RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent
with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to
a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT
represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.

papers.title: Analysing Neural Language Models: Contextual Decomposition Reveals\n Default Reasoning in Number and Gender Assignment
papers.research_question: How do neural language models (specifically LSTMs) process grammatical phenomena such as number agreement and gender anaphora resolution? What information do they base their decisions on, and do they exhibit default reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Generalised Contextual Decomposition (GCD), a method to decompose LSTM predictions into contributions from input phrases and model biases, and uses it to reveal that LSTM language models employ default reasoning for number and gender assignment, with singular and masculine as defaults encoded in the model weights.
papers.conclusion: GCD is a powerful method for analyzing LSTM language models, revealing default reasoning in number and gender assignment, and can be extended to other models and improved with better Shapley value approximations.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models exhibit a default reasoning effect: singular and masculine are default categories hard-coded in the model weights.
For number agreement, plural verb predictions depend strongly on the subject, while singular verb predictions rely more on other sentence elements and model intercepts.
For gender anaphora, the model has a male default bias; predicting female pronouns requires explicit evidence from female referents.
The model shows gender bias in stereotypical gender roles: male-stereotyped job titles lead to male pronoun preference, but female-stereotyped job titles do not lead to a female preference.
GCD enables detailed analysis of anaphora resolution in language models, pinpointing where and how resolution takes place.
future_direction: Extending GCD to attention-based models
Improving the gate factorisation with better Shapley value approximators
Exploring the axiomatic approach to relate GCD to other explanation methods
papers.abstract:
Extensive research has recently shown that recurrent neural language models
are able to process a wide range of grammatical phenomena. How these models are
able to perform these remarkable feats so well, however, is still an open
question. To gain more insight into what information LSTMs base their decisions
on, we propose a generalisation of Contextual Decomposition (GCD). In
particular, this setup enables us to accurately distil which part of a
prediction stems from semantic heuristics, which part truly emanates from
syntactic cues and which part arise from the model biases themselves instead.
We investigate this technique on tasks pertaining to syntactic agreement and
co-reference resolution and discover that the model strongly relies on a
default reasoning effect to perform these tasks.

papers.title: LinguaLens: Towards Interpreting Linguistic Mechanisms of Large Language Models via Sparse Auto-Encoder
papers.research_question: Can we identify the minimal components within an LLM responsible for specific linguistic processing abilities? Can we comprehensively model the internal linguistic functionalities of the model?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LINGUALENS, a framework using Sparse Auto-Encoders to interpret linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, revealing intrinsic representations of linguistic knowledge, cross-layer and cross-lingual distribution patterns, and enabling control of model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LINGUALENS provides a systematic framework for interpreting linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, showing that they encode structured linguistic knowledge and enabling more interpretable and controllable language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LINGUALENS effectively identifies linguistic features in SAE space, with metrics like FRC showing strong correlations.
